findings.summary: The CLEAN (non-faulting) RETURN of the three verbs that DO fault -- stat, get and list -- is entirely unconstrained. theVerbsThatInjectNOTHINGStillDELEGATEFaithfully covers put, getRange and delete; theREADSideFaultsToo only asserts that stat/get/list THROW when unreachable fires; everyClassDrawsOnEVERYFaultingCall calls quiet.stat("a"), quiet.get("a").close() and quiet.list("", null, 10) purely for their effect on drawCounts and never looks at what came back. Every read-back assertion in both files reads the BACKING store (read(backing, ...), backing.stat(...)), never the decorator. MEASURED, three mutants applied one at a time to the staged file with `--rerun-tasks --no-build-cache` after deleting sequencer/build/test-results/test, all 20 tests green (exit 0, killedby=[]): (1) FaultInjectingStore.java:242 `return delegate.stat(k);` -> `return Optional.empty();`; (2) :250 `return delegate.get(k);` -> `return new ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[0]);`; (3) :293 `return delegate.list(p, a, m);` -> `return ListPage.last(List.of());`. This is the same defect class the author has now closed three times on the write side -- round-7's zeroed putIfAbsent payload, round-8's clean putIfAbsent payload and clean putIfMatch version -- arriving through the read door, and the read side is the more consequential half: recover's chain walk is list + get + stat, so a decorator whose clean list returns an empty page makes every recovery see an empty chain and manufactures verbatim the I2 rewind M4.16 spent three rounds diagnosing. The author's own comment at :317-324 states the principle exactly ("a decorator that is wrong on the verbs it does not fault is a decorator that quietly changes the baseline every faulted run is compared against") and then stops three verbs short of it. It is also not merely hypothetical: the M4.13 row commits to teaching list/get/stat about WHICH pod is calling and to adding delayed writes and reordered completions, so the next hand edits exactly these three method bodies. Not disclosed either: the row's "NOT covered" sentence names close, multipart and capabilities, and names "the three read verbs" under COVERED -- true only of their throwing path -- so a reader is told the opposite of what the mutants show. The fix is about eight lines inside the existing clean-path test: store.stat("p") is present, reading store.get("p") yields "hello", store.list("p", null, 10) contains the key.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.19/M4.20 land and the sweep drives LocalSequencer.recover through this decorator. Any edit that breaks a clean read return -- M4.13's per-pod plumbing narrowing a list page, an early return added while wiring a delay, a getRange-style bounds slip -- leaves all 20 tests in this commit green. The sweep then reports empty or truncated chains and offsets resuming at 0 for every seed, which is indistinguishable from M4.16's unsealed-ancestor I2 violation, and the next several rounds are spent diagnosing the protocol for a defect the harness fabricated. That is precisely the failure mode the ambiguousPut conditionality tests were added in round 7 to prevent, on the verbs recovery actually consists of.

findings.summary: Confirming the production reviewer's minor independently: theInjectedRecordIsASNAPSHOTACallerCannotMutate pins the UNMODIFIABLE half of its name and not the SNAPSHOT half. MEASURED: FaultInjectingStore.java:125 `return List.copyOf(injected);` -> `return java.util.Collections.unmodifiableList(injected);` leaves all 20 tests green (exit 0, killedby=[]), because the only assertion is that add() throws UnsupportedOperationException, which an unmodifiable VIEW does too. So the reviewer's read is right. On whether it matters given the diff's own helpers: it does not, today, and I checked rather than assumed -- callsWhereOnly (StreamsTest:144-150) and firedIndexesWith (:204-208) both re-call store.injected() on every iteration and consume it before the next faulting call, tracking progress with an int `seen` rather than by holding a prior list, and kindsFor (:292) maps to a fresh list immediately. Nothing in either file holds a returned list across a subsequent fault, which is the only way a view and a copy differ. Hence minor rather than major: the mutant is real but no current consumer observes it. Two things keep it worth recording. The javadoc at :30-34 makes injected() the file's stated reason for existing ("the only defence is being able to ASSERT that a given run actually saw a given fault"), and a caller that captures injected() before a phase and compares after -- the obvious shape for M4.20's per-phase attribution, and the shape M4.13's "at least one seed where this class changes the outcome" reporting wants -- silently gets two references to the same growing list and compares it against itself. And the test's NAME will be read as having settled the question.
findings.failure_scenario: A future hand simplifies List.copyOf to Collections.unmodifiableList, or returns the field wrapped, and every test passes. M4.20's driver then captures injected() before a takeover and after, finds the two lists equal because they are the same object, and reports zero faults during the phase -- the silent-simulator failure the class javadoc names, produced by the accessor rather than by a probability. Bounded because it needs a new consumer to appear; unbounded in the sense that the test whose name promises to have checked it will not.

findings.summary: drawCounts()'s defensive copy has no test at all, which is the same class as TR2 one accessor over. MEASURED: :179 `return Map.copyOf(drawCounts);` -> `return drawCounts;` leaves all 20 tests green (exit 0, killedby=[]). everyClassDrawsOnEVERYFaultingCall asserts the map's CONTENTS at two points but never that the returned map is independent of the live TreeMap, so a caller can both mutate the counter and watch it move underneath a held reference. Minor, and lower than TR2, for two honest reasons: the row's covered-list claims "the immutability of the record" (singular, and the record is Injected), so this one is not over-claimed by any prose in the diff; and drawCounts is a diagnostic whose only asserted use is inside this file. Recorded because the counter is the mechanism the file itself argues is the ONLY way to see a deleted alignment draw (:137-146), so its accessor is load-bearing for criterion 1's attribution rather than incidental.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.13 edits putIfMatch's two result-discarding draws, as the javadoc at :143-146 anticipates, and reads drawCounts() into an assertion helper that also happens to sort or merge into the map it was given. The counter is corrupted in place, subsequent count assertions in this file compare against a map the test itself perturbed, and the one check that can see a missing draw becomes the check that hides one.

answer_to_author: Rounds 7 and 8 are genuinely closed, and I verified each rather than taking it on the summary. All three round-7 majors die on the exact tests added for them, one test each, no overlap: delegate.put on the ambiguous putIfAbsent landing -> anAmbiguousPutIfAbsentSTILLLOSESToAnOccupiedSlot; delegate.put dropping the version on the ambiguous putIfMatch landing -> anAmbiguousPutIfMatchSTILLLOSESToASTALEVersionAndLandsNothing; new byte[read(body).length] on the faulted putIfAbsent payload -> anAmbiguousPutIfAbsentWRITESTHECALLERSExactBytes... And theCLEANPathWritesTheCALLERSExactBytesAndHONOURSTheVersion carries all three clean-path mutants by itself: zeroed clean putIfAbsent payload, Optional.of(delegate.put(k, b)) on the clean putIfMatch, and Optional.empty() on the clean putIfMatch. The round-6/7 kills have not regressed either -- twelve further mutants all died, and I name them so you can see the surface I probed: getRange bounds swapped and delete made a no-op (theVerbsThatInjectNOTHING...), put ignoring its body (same), the duplicate's second conditional write deleted and the caller handed the retry's Optional instead of the first's (aDUPLICATEDPut...), the unreachable key blanked on putIfAbsent (EVERYClassRecordsWHICHKey...), the Faults guard body disabled (aProbabilityOUTSIDE...), scramble reverted to seed * 3 + stream and scramble ignoring `stream` altogether (theTHREEFaultStreams... and, for the second, eachClassIsWIRED... too), the p == 0 early return restored and putIfMatch's alignment draws moved below its ambiguous throw and stat re-wired onto the ambiguous stream (all three -> everyClassDrawsOnEVERYFaultingCall...). Two surviving mutants are DISCLOSED and I am not counting them against you: swapping the ambiguousPut/duplicatePut labels in countDraw survives exactly as :148-158 says it must, and close() made a no-op survives exactly as the row's NOT-covered sentence says. The rung-2 correction on the countDraw fixability note reads right to me: a named stream removes the re-derivation but a construction site still pairs a name with a scramble index by hand, so the bad state stays representable. That leaves one thing I am asking you to close, and it is small. TR1 is the third appearance of one defect class -- a line executed without its result constrained -- and the two earlier appearances were both accepted as blocking-grade on this same task. The read side is where it matters most, because recover IS list plus get plus stat, so a clean list returning an empty page makes the sweep report M4.16's rewind for every seed with the harness as the author. Eight lines inside theVerbsThatInjectNOTHINGStillDELEGATEFaithfully close it: assert store.stat("p") is present, that reading store.get("p") gives back "hello", and that store.list("p", null, 10) contains the key. While you are there, the row's NOT-covered sentence should gain stat/get/list's clean returns if you choose to leave any of them, because as written it names "the three read verbs" under COVERED and that is true only of their throwing path. TR2 and TR3 are minors and rule 11 applies to them: they land as they are, or as a row, and I would not spend a tenth round on them -- fixing a minor buys a new round whose surface is the prose the fix added, which this task has already paid for twice. If you touch TR2 at all, the cheaper move is renaming the test to what it actually checks rather than adding the snapshot assertion, since no consumer needs snapshot semantics until M4.20 does.
